title: I shipped an idle game to Google Play built with an AI team. Here is what that actually took.
author: ScrywareDev
selftext:
The game is Doomsday Tycoon, an idle clicker where you build a villain empire. You tap for Loot, buy enterprises, hire henchmen, and work through six lairs toward 100% World Domination. Heroes raid your lair and you fight them off in a short dodge fight. When a lair is done you Fake Your Death, prestige, and start the next one carrying permanent buffs with you. It went live on Google Play this month, free with ads and in-app purchases.



I am a solo dev. The team that built it is me plus AI agents, and I want to be plain about how that worked, because it is not "type a prompt, receive a game."



My job is the calls. I decide the design, the economy numbers, what gets cut, and what is good enough to ship. The agents write the code, draw the art, and run the tests. Everything passes in front of me before it goes out. When an agent tells me something is done, my actual job is checking whether that is true. Agents are confident when they should not be, and catching that is most of the work some days.



The art was the hardest part, and it is where I expect the most skepticism here. Generated pixel art drifts. A character looks right in one frame and wrong in the next, hands grow extra fingers, the style slides around between sessions. What fixed it for us was training a LoRA on our own approved art. We took the henchman sprites I had already signed off on, trained a small model on them locally on my own GPU, and generated new characters in that same style from then on. We also locked plain style rules: chunky pixels, silhouette first, a small palette, thick outlines. Every frame still gets a quality pass by eye. Extra limbs get a sprite rejected, same as they would from a human artist.



The code is a native Android app written in Kotlin. Agents built it in pieces, feature by feature, with automated checks run headless before anything merged. Sound effects are synthesized, not composed. There is no composer and no art department. There is me, checking work at the end of every step.



Launch taught me that the store listing is its own job. Screenshots, the description, the icon. Getting those right took days, not an afternoon, and I am still redoing pieces of it. Right now I am running a feedback round: 20 codes for the game's No Ads pass, given privately to people who send helpful feedback directly to us, good or bad. It is not tied to reviews or ratings in any way. The first suggestions were a tutorial glossary and a purchase tier between 10x and 100x, and both were fair points I had not thought hard enough about. The glossary is being built now.



What AI did not do: it did not decide what game to make, it did not set the prices, and it did not tell me when something was fun. It also did not remove the boring parts. It moved them. Less time typing code, more time reviewing, rejecting, and re-checking.



I do not have a big number to put in the title. The game is live, it is small, and it is still being worked on. I am posting because the process posts in this sub helped me when I was figuring out how to work this way, and this is ours, honestly told.



Happy to answer questions about the agent workflow, the LoRA training, or the launch side.



AI disclosure, since this sub runs on being upfront about it: code, yes, written with AI agents and reviewed by me. Graphics, yes, generated with AI tools and our own trained style model, checked frame by frame. Text, yes, drafted with AI help and edited by me. Sounds, yes, synthesized.



Game link, if you want to see what came out the other end: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.scryware.doomsdaytycoon](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.scryware.doomsdaytycoon)



My site, with the other apps and games I am working on: [https://scryware.io](https://scryware.io)
